nodes.label: Uruk and the First Cities
nodes.full: The preceding age — the invention of the city, of writing, of the temple estate and the sealing bureaucracy — whose institutions and script the Early Dynastic cities inherit and elaborate. See uruk-3800bc-2900bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio uruk-3800bc-2900bc.

nodes.label: The Akkadian Empire
nodes.full: Sargon of Akkad, who defeats Lugalzagesi and builds the first lasting territorial empire over Sumer and beyond — the age this folio ends on. See akkad-2334bc-2004bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio akkad-2334bc-2004bc.

nodes.label: Elam and the Iranian highlands
nodes.full: Susa on the plain and Anshan in the mountains — a trading partner for tin, silver, timber, stone and slaves, a raider of Sumerian cities, and a target of Sumerian campaigns.
nodes.src: background — Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999).

nodes.label: The Gulf — Dilmun, Magan, Meluhha
nodes.full: The sea route south: Dilmun the entrepôt (Bahrain), Magan the copper land (Oman), and Meluhha (the Indus). See the folios dilmun-3000bc-1200bc and magan-3000bc-1200bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folios dilmun-3000bc-1200bc, magan-3000bc-1200bc.

nodes.label: Mari and Ebla
nodes.full: The Euphrates-corridor and Syrian cities — Mari controlling the river traffic, Ebla with its Semitic archive written in the Sumerian scribal system — that show the Sumerian cultural world reaching to the Mediterranean.
nodes.src: background — Margueron, 'Mari' (2004); Pettinato, 'The Archives of Ebla' (1981).

nodes.label: Etana and the kings before history
nodes.full: The Sumerian King List opens after the Flood with kingship 'lowered from heaven' to Kish, and a line of rulers with fantastic reign-lengths — among them Etana, 'the shepherd who ascended to heaven and made firm all the lands', a hero of later legend. None can be verified, but the list encodes a claim: that Kish held the first legitimate kingship over the land.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Sumerian King List' (AS 11, 1939); the Etana legend edited by J. V. Kinnier Wilson (1985).

nodes.label: En-mebaragesi and Aga — the record begins
nodes.full: En-mebaragesi of Kish is the earliest Sumerian ruler attested by his own inscriptions — two stone fragments naming him — and the King List credits him with carrying off the weapons of Elam. His son Aga besieged Uruk and features in the Sumerian poem 'Gilgamesh and Aga', in which the men of Uruk refuse to submit. With them, Sumerian history leaves legend for documented fact.
nodes.src: En-mebaragesi vase inscriptions in Douglas Frayne, RIME 1 (2008); 'Gilgamesh and Aga' edited by Dina Katz (1993).

nodes.label: 'King of Kish' — the title of overlordship
nodes.full: Whichever Sumerian ruler claimed leadership over the whole land took the title lugal Kiš, 'king of Kish' — worn by rulers of Ur, Lagash, Uruk and Umma who never governed Kish itself, and later by Sargon of Akkad. Kish, commanding the narrow neck where the Tigris and Euphrates run closest, had become the symbol of hegemony over Sumer as a whole.
nodes.src: William Hallo, 'Early Mesopotamian Royal Titles' (1957); the title's use tracked across the Presargonic inscriptions (Cooper 1986).

nodes.label: Mesalim, the overlord who drew the line
nodes.full: King Mesalim of Kish was acknowledged across southern Sumer: he dedicated a mace-head at Lagash and a bowl at Adab, and — most consequentially — he surveyed and set a boundary stele between Lagash and Umma along the divine command of Ishtaran. That line, and its repeated violation, drives the next century and a half of southern politics.
nodes.src: Mesalim's dedications in Frayne, RIME 1; his boundary settlement reconstructed in Jerrold Cooper, 'Reconstructing History: The Lagash–Umma Border Conflict' (1983).

nodes.label: Gilgamesh of Uruk
nodes.full: The King List makes Bilgames — Gilgamesh — the fifth king of Uruk's first dynasty, and a later tradition credits him with building the city wall and the Ninlil temple at Nippur. No contemporary inscription of his survives, but a ruler of that name and rough date is plausible, and by the Ur III period he was a god, a judge of the dead, and the hero of a poem cycle that became the world's first epic.
nodes.src: The King List (Jacobsen 1939); the Sumerian Gilgamesh poems and the epic in Andrew George, 'The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic' (2003).

nodes.label: Mesannepada and the First Dynasty of Ur
nodes.full: Mesannepada, 'king of Ur, king of Kish', is the first ruler of Ur fixed by contemporary evidence — his name inscribed on a lapis bead found at Mari, five hundred kilometres away, a measure of the reach of his contacts. His predecessors Meskalamdug and Akalamdug are known chiefly from the gold and the graves of Ur's Royal Cemetery, which belongs to this dynasty's world.
nodes.src: Mesannepada bead and inscriptions in Frayne, RIME 1; the dynasty and the cemetery in Leonard Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II: The Royal Cemetery' (1934).

nodes.label: Puabi of Ur
nodes.full: In one of the great tombs of the Royal Cemetery lay a woman about forty, adorned with a headdress of gold leaves and lapis, her name and the title nin — 'lady' or 'queen' — cut on three cylinder seals beside her. Buried with her were dozens of attendants, wagons and oxen. Whether Puabi ruled in her own right, was a king's consort, or was a high priestess of the moon-god is unresolved; that she held real standing is not.
nodes.src: Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934); re-analysis in Richard Zettler & Lee Horne (eds.), 'Treasures from the Royal Tombs of Ur' (1998).

nodes.label: Ur-Nanshe founds the house of Lagash
nodes.full: Ur-Nanshe of Lagash built temples, dug canals, imported timber by ship from Dilmun, and left a series of dedication reliefs — one showing him carrying a builder's basket of clay on his head, his wife and named sons around him. His reign begins the richest documentary record of the Early Dynastic age: the archives of Lagash, from which most of what we know of ED society is drawn.
nodes.src: Ur-Nanshe inscriptions and reliefs in Frayne, RIME 1, and Jerrold Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986).

nodes.label: Eannatum, 'who subjugated all the lands'
nodes.full: Eannatum, Ur-Nanshe's grandson, made Lagash briefly the strongest power in Sumer: he crushed Umma and reimposed the border, and campaigned against Ur, Uruk, Kish, Elam, Mari and the Iranian highlands, taking the title 'king of Kish'. His victory over Umma is carved on the Stele of the Vultures, the first war monument. His empire did not outlast him.
nodes.src: Eannatum's inscriptions (the 'Stele of the Vultures' text, the Mesilim cone) in Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986); Frayne, RIME 1.

nodes.label: Enannatum I and Entemena
nodes.full: Eannatum's brother Enannatum I and nephew Entemena held Lagash at its most prosperous. Entemena's inscribed clay cone lays out the whole Umma dispute from Mesalim onward as a legal brief, and he made a treaty of 'brotherhood' with Lugal-kinishe-dudu of Uruk — the earliest known interstate parity treaty. His silver libation vase, worked with the lion-headed eagle of Ningirsu, is a masterpiece of ED metalwork.
nodes.src: Entemena cone and vase in Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986) and 'Reconstructing History' (1983); the vase in the Louvre.

nodes.label: Urukagina and the reform edict
nodes.full: Urukagina (his name may read Uru-inim-gina), coming to power in Lagash outside the ruling line, issued a text describing abuses he had ended — officials seizing the property of the poor, priests overcharging for burials, the palace encroaching on temple and citizen land — and claimed to have made a covenant with the god Ningirsu 'that the powerful man would not oppress the orphan and the widow'. It is the first recorded programme of social reform.
nodes.src: The reform texts (Ukg. 1, 4–6, 15) in Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986); analysis in Samuel Noah Kramer, 'The Sumerians' (1963) and Piotr Steinkeller.

nodes.label: Lugalzagesi unites the land
nodes.full: Lugalzagesi, governor of Umma, broke Lagash and burned its temples, then took Uruk and made it his capital, claiming from Enlil at Nippur kingship over all Sumer 'from the Lower Sea, along the Tigris and Euphrates, to the Upper Sea'. It was the first time one man ruled the whole of Sumer. Twenty-odd years later Sargon of Akkad defeated him and led him in a neck-stock to the gate of Enlil.
nodes.src: Lugalzagesi's Nippur vase inscription in Frayne, RIME 1; his fall recorded in Sargon's inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 2).

nodes.label: The Sumerian King List and rotating kingship
nodes.full: The King List presents Sumerian history as a single kingship passing from one city to the next — Kish, then Uruk, then Ur, then elsewhere — never held by two cities at once, moving by the will of the gods. Real Early Dynastic Sumer was a scatter of rival states holding power simultaneously. The List is not a chronicle but a charter: an argument that legitimate rule over the land is one and indivisible, and belongs to whoever currently holds it.
nodes.src: Jacobsen, 'The Sumerian King List' (1939); the ideological reading in Piotr Michalowski, 'History as Charter' (JAOS 1983).

nodes.label: Lagash against Umma — the first recorded war
nodes.full: For some five generations Lagash and Umma fought over the Gu'edena, a strip of fertile canal-fed land on their border. King Mesalim of Kish had set a boundary stele there; Umma repeatedly ploughed across it and diverted its water, Lagash repeatedly drove them back. It is the earliest war anywhere for which both the cause and the course are written down — by the Lagash side, at length and with grievance.
nodes.src: Reconstructed from the Lagash inscriptions in Jerrold Cooper, 'Reconstructing History: The Lagash–Umma Border Conflict' (1983).

nodes.label: The Stele of the Vultures
nodes.full: Eannatum's limestone victory stele carries the war on two registers. On the divine side the god Ningirsu holds a net full of struggling enemies and brains them with a mace. On the human side Eannatum leads a tight block of helmeted, shielded spearmen marching over a heap of the enemy dead while vultures fly off with severed heads. It is the earliest image of a disciplined infantry formation — the phalanx — and of a state at organised war.
nodes.src: Louvre; the definitive study is Irene Winter, 'After the Battle is Over: The Stele of the Vultures and the Beginning of Historical Narrative in the Art of the Ancient Near East' (1985).

nodes.label: The war-wagons of the Standard of Ur
nodes.full: An inlaid wooden box from a royal grave at Ur shows the Early Dynastic army: four-wheeled battle-wagons drawn by onagers rolling over fallen enemies, files of spearmen in studded cloaks, axemen, and naked bound prisoners driven before the king. The other face shows the victory feast. Together they picture the two things a Sumerian ruler was for — to win the war and to preside over the plenty that followed.
nodes.src: British Museum (BM 121201); Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934); military reading in Robert Rollinger and in the essays in Zettler & Horne (1998).

nodes.label: The contest for the leadership of the land
nodes.full: Behind the Gu'edena quarrel ran a larger, shifting struggle for primacy — Kish against Uruk in 'Gilgamesh and Aga', Ur's kings claiming Kish, Eannatum of Lagash storming across the whole south and into Elam, Enshakushana of Uruk sacking Kish and taking its king prisoner. No city held the lead for long, and the title everyone wanted, 'king of Kish', was worth having precisely because it was contested.
nodes.src: The hegemony sequence in the Presargonic inscriptions (Cooper 1986; Frayne, RIME 1); overview in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'A History of the Ancient Near East' (2016).

nodes.label: The sack of Lagash and the lament for it
nodes.full: When Lugalzagesi of Umma overran Lagash he burned the shrines of Girsu, Antasura, Nina and the rest, and carried off their silver and precious stones. A scribe of the defeated Urukagina wrote a short text cataloguing each act of desecration and ending: 'The man of Umma, having sacked Lagash, has committed a sin against Ningirsu... May his goddess Nisaba make him bear the sin.' It is the earliest formal indictment of an enemy for sacrilege in war.
nodes.src: The 'Lament for Lagash' (Ukg. 16) in Cooper, 'Presargonic Inscriptions' (1986); discussed in Piotr Michalowski, 'The Lamentation over the Destruction of Sumer and Ur' (1989), intro.

nodes.label: The walled city and the guarded gate
nodes.full: Every Early Dynastic city of consequence was walled — Uruk's great circuit was already ancient — and the temple itself might be a fortress, as at Khafajah, where the oval sanctuary sat inside its own double enclosure. The city gate was where courts sat, deals were struck and treaties sworn, a defended threshold that was also the city's public room.
nodes.src: Khafajah Temple Oval in Pinhas Delougaz, 'The Temple Oval at Khafajah' (OIP 53, 1940); ED fortification surveyed in Roger Matthews, 'The Archaeology of Mesopotamia' (2003).

nodes.label: The ensí, the lugal and the god's estate
nodes.full: A Sumerian ruler was in principle the manager of his city-god's household. The commonest title, ensí, means roughly 'governor' or 'steward'; lugal, 'big man', claimed more — kingship, often over other cities too. The ruler held the land as the god's tenant and answered to the god for it. Beside the temple, a distinct royal residence, the é-gal or 'big house', was now taking shape as an institution in its own right.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'Early Political Development in Mesopotamia' (ZA 1957); Piotr Steinkeller, 'On Rulers, Priests and Sacred Marriage' (1999).

nodes.label: The palace encroaches on the temple estate
nodes.full: The Lagash archives show the city-god's estate — the households of Ningirsu and the goddess Bau — as the dominant landholder and employer. But under the last kings the royal household and the queen's household were absorbing temple land, appointing their own men to priesthoods, and taxing what had been the god's. Urukagina's reform text is one side's account of that quarrel between crown and cult.
nodes.src: Gebhard Selz, 'Untersuchungen zur Götterwelt des altsumerischen Stadtstaates von Lagaš' (1995); the estate figures in Benjamin Foster, 'A New Look at the Sumerian Temple State' (1981).

nodes.label: The é-mí — the queen's household
nodes.full: The 'house of the woman', é-mí, was the estate of the ruler's wife — under Baranamtara, wife of Lugalanda, and Shasha, wife of Urukagina, a great agricultural and textile enterprise with well over a thousand dependent workers and its own detailed archive. Sumerian queens conducted diplomacy by gift-exchange with other courts and endowed temples in their own name. It is the clearest early evidence for institutional economic power in women's hands.
nodes.src: Kazuya Maekawa, 'The Development of the é-mí in Lagash' (1973); the Baranamtara and Shasha archives, published across the Presargonic Lagash text corpus.

nodes.label: Weight, measure and the sealed standard
nodes.full: Trade and taxation ran on shared units — the shekel, mina and talent for weight; the sila and gur for grain; the sar for area — checked against official stone weights and sealed measuring vessels. Rulers advertised 'just' weights as a mark of good government, and Urukagina's reforms include a promise to stop officials cheating with false measures.
nodes.src: Marvin Powell, 'Masse und Gewichte' (Reallexikon der Assyriologie VII, 1990); the ideology of just measures in the reform texts (Cooper 1986).

nodes.label: Law without a code
nodes.full: No Early Dynastic law code survives, and there may have been none — but the legal order is visible everywhere else: engraved stone tablets recording sales of land before named witnesses (the 'Blau monuments' and their kin), the settlement of lawsuits, oaths sworn by the king and the city-god, and rulers' claims to have protected the weak against the strong. Written law codes come two centuries later, at Ur.
nodes.src: Claus Wilcke, 'Early Ancient Near Eastern Law' (2007); the archaic land-sale documents (kudurrus) catalogued by Ignace Gelb, Piotr Steinkeller & Robert Whiting, 'Earliest Land Tenure Systems in the Near East' (1991).

nodes.label: Nippur, the Tummal and the league of cities
nodes.full: The southern cities — 'Sumer', ki-en-gi — seem to have shared cultic duties toward Enlil at Nippur, taking turns to maintain his sanctuary and the shrine of the Tummal, whose upkeep the later 'Tummal Inscription' records ruler by ruler. Nippur held no army and conquered nobody; it was the neutral ground where a claim to lead the land was ratified. Whether this amounted to a formal 'Kengir League' is debated.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Tummal Inscription' (JCS 1953); the league idea and its critics in Piotr Michalowski, 'Mental Maps and Ideology' (1993).

nodes.label: Enlil of Nippur, giver of kingship
nodes.full: Enlil, whose house the E-kur stood at Nippur, was the executive of the divine assembly — the god who set destinies and, above all, who granted or withdrew the kingship of the land. Rulers from every rival city sought his sanction and rebuilt his temple. Nippur itself stayed out of politics, and that is exactly why its blessing was worth having: it belonged to no faction.
nodes.src: Nippur excavations published in the OIP series (McCown, Haines, Gibson); Enlil's role in W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Creation Myths' (2013) and Jacobsen, 'The Treasures of Darkness' (1976).

nodes.label: The city and its god
nodes.full: Each Sumerian city belonged to a deity — Nanna the moon at Ur, Inanna at Uruk, Enki at Eridu, Ningirsu at Lagash, Shara at Umma — who lived in its main temple, owned much of its land, and was fed, clothed and entertained by the citizens as a great householder. To be a citizen was to be part of the god's estate; a war between cities was, in the telling, a quarrel between their gods.
nodes.src: Gebhard Selz on the Lagash pantheon (1995); the 'divine household' model in Jacobsen, 'The Treasures of Darkness' (1976).

nodes.label: The pantheon and the god-lists
nodes.full: The tablets from Fara and Abu Salabikh include the earliest god-lists — hundreds of divine names set in a fixed order that ranks the pantheon, headed by An the sky, Enlil, Enki and the mother-goddess. To list the gods in order was itself a theological act: it fixed who outranked whom in the assembly that governed the universe, and the ordering barely changed for two thousand years.
nodes.src: The Fara god-list edited by Manfred Krebernik; the Abu Salabikh texts in Robert Biggs, 'Inscriptions from Tell Abu Salabikh' (OIP 99, 1974).

nodes.label: The votive statue — the eternal worshipper
nodes.full: An Early Dynastic worshipper could commission a small stone image of himself — standing, hands clasped at the chest, enormous eyes inlaid with shell and dark stone, sometimes inscribed 'it offers prayers' — and set it in the god's temple to stand before the deity forever on his behalf. A cache of a dozen, buried under the floor of the Square Temple at Tell Asmar, is the type-find.
nodes.src: Henri Frankfort, 'Sculpture of the Third Millennium B.C. from Tell Asmar and Khafajah' (OIP 44, 1939); Jean Evans, 'The Lives of Sumerian Sculpture' (2012).

nodes.label: The death pits of Ur
nodes.full: In the largest tombs of Ur, the ruler was buried with a household that went into the grave too — soldiers at the door, grooms with the wagon-oxen, women in gold headdresses, musicians with their lyres, dozens of people laid out in rows. Woolley thought they took poison willingly; forensic re-study of the skulls found blunt-force wounds, and traces of heating and mercury that suggest the bodies were treated and displayed. Nothing like it recurs in Mesopotamia.
nodes.src: Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934); the forensic re-analysis in Aubrey Baadsgaard, Janet Monge & Richard Zettler, 'Bludgeoned, Burned, and Beautified' (2011) and their Antiquity paper.

nodes.label: The festival year
nodes.full: The temple set the calendar: monthly offerings, the great seasonal festivals, the barley-eating and malt-eating feasts of Ningirsu at Lagash, the Tummal festival at Nippur, and at the turn of the year a rite in which the ruler, as the god's steward, was joined to the goddess to renew the land's fertility. Religion here was less a set of beliefs than a year-round schedule of feeding and honouring the divine landlords.
nodes.src: The Lagash festival calendar in Gebhard Selz (1995); the year-rite ('sacred marriage') debated in Steinkeller, 'On Rulers, Priests and Sacred Marriage' (1999).

nodes.label: The first literature — Fara and Abu Salabikh
nodes.full: The tablet hoards of Shuruppak and Abu Salabikh contain the oldest written literature: hymns praising the temples of the land, a hymn to the temple of Kesh, praise-poems to the gods, and a father's book of instructions to his son. Some tablets carry the names of the scribes who wrote them — a few of those names are Semitic, not Sumerian — the first authors known by name.
nodes.src: Robert Biggs, 'Inscriptions from Tell Abu Salabikh' (OIP 99, 1974); Bendt Alster, 'Wisdom of Ancient Sumer' (2005); the Kesh Temple Hymn edited by Gene Gragg (1969).

nodes.label: The dedication plaque and the banquet
nodes.full: A recurring Early Dynastic object is the square limestone plaque, pierced in the centre for a peg, carved in low relief and fixed to a temple wall. Ur-Nanshe's shows him carrying a basket of building clay with his named children around him; others show the ruler and his consort seated at a feast, cup raised, servants and musicians attending. The banquet — the shared drink that seals an order — is the signature Sumerian subject.
nodes.src: The Ur-Nanshe plaque in the Louvre; ED plaques catalogued in Ursula Seidl and in the al-Hiba reports of Donald Hansen.

nodes.label: The Standard of Ur and the art of inlay
nodes.full: Sumerian craftsmen built pictures from cut pieces of white shell, blue lapis lazuli and red limestone bedded in bitumen over a wooden core. The technique carries the war-and-peace panels of the 'Standard' of Ur, the soundboxes of the lyres, gaming boards and box lids — a jewel-like, high-contrast style, labour-intensive and reserved for the temple and the tomb.
nodes.src: British Museum; Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934); technique in Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The lyres of the royal tombs
nodes.full: Several graves at Ur held large lyres and a harp, their soundboxes fronted with a bull's head of gold or copper with a lapis beard, and inlaid panels of animals playing music. Musicians were buried holding them. Reconstructions can be played, and Sumerian texts already name instrument types and musical intervals — the deepest documented root of a musical tradition. The Iraq Museum's lyre was smashed and looted in 2003 and later restored.
nodes.src: Woolley (1934); Maude de Schauensee, 'Two Lyres from Ur' (2002); Anne Kilmer & the 'Sounds from Silence' reconstructions; the 2003 damage documented by the Iraq Museum.

nodes.label: The goldwork of the Ur cemetery
nodes.full: The Royal Cemetery yielded a body of goldsmithing unmatched for two thousand years: Meskalamdug's helmet beaten from a single sheet with the hair and bun rendered in repoussé, a gold dagger with a lapis hilt and filigree sheath, Puabi's leaf-and-flower headdress, granulated beads, and the gold-and-lapis 'Ram in a Thicket'. All of it worked from imported metal and stone by specialists attached to the court.
nodes.src: Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934); Richard Zettler & Lee Horne (eds.), 'Treasures from the Royal Tombs of Ur' (1998).

nodes.label: The contest frieze
nodes.full: The dominant image on Early Dynastic cylinder seals is the endless combat: nude heroes, bull-men and lions gripping and stabbing one another in a frieze that runs unbroken around the seal, with no beginning and no end. Alongside it runs the banquet scene. Between them they cover most of ED glyptic — a small, dense art carried on every official's belt.
nodes.src: Pierre Amiet, 'La glyptique mésopotamienne archaïque' (1980); Edith Porada, 'Corpus of Ancient Near Eastern Seals' I (1948).

nodes.label: Sumerian written in full
nodes.full: By the middle of the third millennium the script could do what the Uruk tablets could not: render the grammar and word-order of spoken Sumerian, and so write a sentence, a curse, a hymn, a law. Signs took on syllabic values to spell out prefixes and endings; the tablet could now hold connected language. Everything Mesopotamia later wrote — letters, epics, treaties, science — depends on this step.
nodes.src: Jerrold Cooper, 'Sumerian and Akkadian' (in Peter Daniels & William Bright, eds., 'The World's Writing Systems', 1996); Piotr Michalowski, 'Sumerian' (2004).

nodes.label: The Instructions of Shuruppak
nodes.full: An old man of Shuruppak instructs his son: do not stand surety for anyone, it will not be repaid; do not buy a donkey that brays too much; do not pass judgement while you are drunk; a slave girl in the house is a quarrel waiting to happen. The oldest wisdom text known, it founds a genre — practical, sceptical, conservative advice — that runs through the Bible's Proverbs to the medieval mirrors for princes.
nodes.src: Bendt Alster, 'The Instructions of Šuruppak' (1974; rev. 'Wisdom of Ancient Sumer', 2005).

nodes.label: The shared scribal curriculum
nodes.full: The same lists — of professions, of place-names, of trees and wooden objects, of birds, of fish — turn up in near-identical form at Shuruppak, at Abu Salabikh, and as far away as Ebla in Syria. Scribes everywhere learned to write by copying this fixed corpus, which means they also learned the same way of sorting the world into ordered kinds. It is a curriculum and a shared cognitive map at once.
nodes.src: Robert Biggs, OIP 99 (1974); Niek Veldhuis, 'History of the Cuneiform Lexical Tradition' (2014); the Ebla parallels in Giovanni Pettinato's editions.

nodes.label: The mathematics of the field and the ration
nodes.full: Early Dynastic scribes computed areas of fields from their sides, divided a lump sum of barley into equal daily rations, worked out how many bricks a wall would need and how many workers a task, and converted freely between the several measuring systems. The full sexagesimal place-value notation lay two or three centuries ahead, but the practical toolkit — and the habit of setting a problem and solving it — was already in daily use.
nodes.src: Eleanor Robson, 'Mathematics in Ancient Iraq: A Social History' (2008), ch. 2; Jöran Friberg's analyses of the ED metro-mathematical texts.

nodes.label: The tablet house and its goddess
nodes.full: Learning to write was a formal apprenticeship in the é-dubba, the 'tablet house': the pupil copied sign-lists and model texts under a teacher, and the craft passed down within scribal families. Writing had its own divine patron, the goddess Nisaba, invoked in the colophons and credited with the reed stylus and the measuring line. A literate class, self-reproducing and self-aware, now existed.
nodes.src: Herman Vanstiphout, 'How Did They Learn Sumerian?' (1979); Niek Veldhuis on Nippur schooling; the goddess Nisaba in W. W. Hallo's studies.

nodes.label: Barley, salt and falling yields
nodes.full: The Girsu archives let the southern farm economy be watched year by year — and they show it degrading. As irrigation without drainage drew salt up into the topsoil, the share of the crop given to salt-tolerant barley rather than wheat climbed toward totality, and recorded yields in the worst districts fell by half over a few generations. It is the earliest environmental decline anyone documented as it happened.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen & Robert Adams, 'Salt and Silt in Ancient Mesopotamian Agriculture' (Science 1958); a sceptical re-reading of the yield figures in Marvin Powell, 'Salt, Seed, and Yields in Sumerian Agriculture' (ZA 1985).

nodes.label: The plough team and the dependent worker
nodes.full: The institutional estates were farmed by standing crews — a seeder-plough, an ox span and about three men to a unit — and by gangs called out for the harvest and the canal work. The able-bodied dependent man (guruš) and woman (geme) worked for monthly rations of barley, oil and wool, listed by name, and could be moved between field, workshop and towpath as the estate required.
nodes.src: Kazuya Maekawa's studies of Presargonic Lagash labour; the ration-worker category in I. J. Gelb, 'The Ancient Mesopotamian Ration System' (JNES 1965).

nodes.label: The great flocks and the wool office
nodes.full: The temple households of Lagash ran flocks numbering into the tens of thousands, tracked by a dedicated 'wool office' that recorded each animal, its shearing and its fleece by weight. Wool fed the weaving workshops, and finished cloth was the manufactured good a resource-poor south could ship out in quantity. Sheep, more than grain, were the estates' movable wealth.
nodes.src: The Presargonic Lagash livestock and wool texts; Rosemary Prentice, 'The Exchange of Goods and Services in Pre-Sargonic Lagash' (2010).

nodes.label: The ration and the standard of life
nodes.full: A dependent worker's income was the sà-dug, a monthly measure of barley — roughly 60 litres for an adult man, less for a woman, less again for a child — plus periodic oil and wool. It was enough to live on and little more, and it tied the worker to the institution that paid it. A free citizen with a house-plot and a field stood outside that system; much of Urukagina's reform is about the boundary between the two.
nodes.src: I. J. Gelb, 'The Ancient Mesopotamian Ration System' (JNES 1965); ration scales in the Lagash archives (Maekawa).

nodes.label: The merchants of the Gulf
nodes.full: Ur-Nanshe of Lagash boasted that ships of Dilmun brought him timber, and the archives name the dam-gàr, the merchant — often trading on the temple's or the palace's account — who sailed south for copper and returned with it and with tin, stone and aromatics. Silver, weighed against the shekel, served as the money of account. Long-distance trade was substantially a state enterprise.
nodes.src: A. Leo Oppenheim, 'The Seafaring Merchants of Ur' (JAOS 1954); Daniel Potts, 'The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity' I (1990).

nodes.label: The institutional workshop
nodes.full: The estates ran workshops — a smithy, a carpentry and reed shop, a leather shop, and above all the 'house of the female weavers' with its hundreds of women and children — each under a named overseer, drawing raw materials from the store and returning finished goods against a quota. Craft in the Sumerian city was mostly not a market of independent artisans but a set of departments inside a great household.
nodes.src: ED workshop organisation reconstructed from the Lagash archives; comparanda in Hartmut Waetzoldt's textile-industry studies and Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994).

nodes.label: The battle-wagon and the solid wheel
nodes.full: Early Dynastic armies fielded four- and two-wheeled vehicles drawn by onagers — solid tripartite disc wheels with studded leather tyres, a driver and a spearman, rolling over the enemy line. Model carts, actual wheel remains and vehicle burials survive from Kish, Susa and Tell Agrab, and the Standard of Ur shows them in action. Faster spoked chariots and true horses were still centuries away.
nodes.src: Mary Littauer & Joost Crouwel, 'Wheeled Vehicles and Ridden Animals in the Ancient Near East' (1979); the Kish and Susa vehicle burials.

nodes.label: Tin-bronze and the cast weapon
nodes.full: Smiths learned to alloy copper with a small fraction of tin — harder, tougher and easier to cast than copper alone — and turned out socketed spearheads, shaft-hole and socketed axes, adzes and daggers in two-piece and lost-wax moulds. Every ingredient was imported: the copper from Oman or Anatolia, the tin from somewhere on the Iranian plateau or beyond, a supply line the cities guarded and fought over.
nodes.src: Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994); the tin-source problem in James Muhly's studies.

nodes.label: The arch, the vault and the baked brick
nodes.full: The stone-built chambers of the great Ur tombs were roofed with true corbelled and radial vaults and domes, and drains at al-Ubaid ran under baked-brick arches. Mesopotamian builders had worked out how to span space in brick and stone without timber — knowledge that a treeless land needed, and that grew into the vaulted architecture of later Babylonia.
nodes.src: Woolley, 'Ur Excavations II' (1934), on the tomb vaulting; brick-arch technique in Moorey (1994).

nodes.label: The seagoing boat
nodes.full: The magur and magilum boats that carried the Gulf trade were built of planks sewn together with cord and sealed with bitumen, or of great bundles of reed similarly caulked, propelled by pole and square sail. Sturdy enough for the run to Bahrain and on to the coast of Oman, they made the southern cities a maritime as well as a riverine power.
nodes.src: Boat types in Daniel Potts, 'Mesopotamian Civilization: The Material Foundations' (1997), ch. 5; bitumen-caulked hull remains from Gulf sites (Robert Carter).

nodes.label: The canal network as a weapon
nodes.full: By the Early Dynastic period the south was laced with a maintained hierarchy of main canals, branch canals and field ditches, with weirs and regulators to control the flow, and officials — the canal inspectors — to keep it dredged. The same works were instruments of war: Umma is repeatedly accused of diverting the water of the border canal, and cutting a rival's supply was a recognised act of aggression.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); the water-as-weapon accusations in the Lagash inscriptions (Cooper, 'Reconstructing History', 1983).

nodes.label: Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha
nodes.full: Sumerian and Akkadian texts name three lands reached by sea: Dilmun (Bahrain and the eastern Arabian coast), the entrepôt that supplied dates, 'fish-eyes' (pearls) and 'sweet water'; Magan (Oman), the source of copper and diorite; and Meluhha (the Indus valley), which sent carnelian, ivory, exotic timber and the 'meluhha-bird'. The trade ran on the temple's account and made the Gulf a Sumerian sphere.
nodes.src: Daniel Potts, 'The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity' I (1990); the textual references collected in Potts and in the folios dilmun-3000bc-1200bc and magan-3000bc-1200bc.

nodes.label: The lapis and carnelian roads
nodes.full: Lapis lazuli still came only from Badakhshan, passed westward across the Iranian plateau town by town; long carnelian beads etched with white patterns — an Indus manufacturing technique — reached the graves of Ur; and tin, silver, chlorite and alabaster travelled the same overland routes. The Ur cemetery is, among other things, a map of these networks rendered in stone and metal.
nodes.src: Georgina Herrmann, 'Lapis Lazuli: The Early Phases of its Trade' (Iraq 1968); the etched carnelian beads discussed by Horace Beck and by Massimo Vidale.

nodes.label: Mari and the river to Syria
nodes.full: Mari, on the Euphrates bend where it turns toward Syria, was a Sumerian-culture city that lived off the river traffic — timber, wine, oil, resin and metal moving between Sumer and the north-west, taxed as it passed. Its Early Dynastic palace, its temple of Ishtar with the praying statue of the official Ebih-Il, and a bead of Mesannepada of Ur found in its treasury all show how far the southern world reached up the Euphrates.
nodes.src: André Parrot's excavations, published in the 'Mission archéologique de Mari' series; synthesis in Jean-Claude Margueron, 'Mari: Métropole de l'Euphrate' (2004).

nodes.label: Ebla and the Sumerian scribal sphere
nodes.full: The palace archive of Ebla in northern Syria — thousands of tablets — is written in a Semitic language but by scribes trained in the Sumerian system, using the same sign-lists and school texts as Shuruppak. Ebla traded textiles and metals across the Near East, warred and made peace with Mari, and shows that the intellectual world Sumer had built already stretched from the Gulf to the Mediterranean.
nodes.src: Giovanni Pettinato, 'The Archives of Ebla' (1981); Alfonso Archi's editions and studies of the Ebla texts.

nodes.label: Elam — larder and threat
nodes.full: East of the Tigris lay Elam — Susa on the plain, Anshan in the highlands — by turns a trading partner supplying tin, silver, stone, timber, horses and slaves, a raider that sacked Sumerian cities, and a target of Sumerian campaigns from Eannatum onward. The Sumerians saw the eastern mountains as both the storehouse of what they lacked and the direction from which trouble came.
nodes.src: Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999); the Sumerian–Elamite wars in the Presargonic inscriptions (Frayne, RIME 1).

nodes.label: The city and its territory
nodes.full: By the Early Dynastic period the south had settled into a stable pattern: a dozen cities strung along the branches of the Euphrates, each holding a wedge of irrigated country with its own villages, canal and boundary. Survey shows the population still overwhelmingly inside the walls, the countryside a thin scatter. The 'city and its land' was the unit of politics, economy and identity, and the gaps between city territories were where the wars were fought.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); Adams & Nissen, 'The Uruk Countryside' (1972) for the earlier baseline.

nodes.label: The souring of the southern fields
nodes.full: Generations of watering without drainage in a climate that evaporates hard left a white salt crust on abandoned fields and forced the crop toward barley alone. The damage was local and patchy, not a single collapse, but it was cumulative — and over the following centuries the productive centre of gravity of Mesopotamia drifted north, away from the old Sumerian heartland toward Akkad and Babylon.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen & Robert Adams, 'Salt and Silt' (Science 1958); the northward shift discussed in McGuire Gibson, 'Violation of Fallow and Engineered Disaster in Mesopotamian Civilization' (1974).

nodes.label: Sumerian and Akkadian
nodes.full: From the first legible records, Semitic personal names — the language later called Akkadian — appear beside Sumerian ones, more thickly in the north around Kish. The two languages shared a script, borrowed words freely, and named the land together as 'Sumer and Akkad'. Whether the 'Sumerians' were ever a distinct people rather than simply the speakers of one of two long-mingled languages is an old and unresolved question.
nodes.src: Jerrold Cooper, 'Sumer, Sumerisch' (Reallexikon der Assyriologie); Gonzalo Rubio, 'On the Alleged Pre-Sumerian Substratum' (JCS 1999).

nodes.label: The reach of the Sumerian world
nodes.full: There was no Sumerian state larger than a city, but there was a Sumerian world: the same wedge-script, the same great gods, the same school lists, the same art of the votive statue and the inlaid lyre, the same weights, from the head of the Gulf up the Euphrates to Mari and Ebla, east to Susa, and north to Assur and Nineveh, whose earliest temples are built in the southern style.
nodes.src: The spread of southern-style temple architecture and material culture surveyed in Michael Roaf, 'Cultural Atlas of Mesopotamia' (1990); the Ebla and Mari evidence (Archi; Margueron).

nodes.label: The dependent worker's year
nodes.full: For the guruš and the geme — the able-bodied dependent man and woman on the estate's books — life was a round of assigned tasks: ploughing and reaping in season, hauling on the canal banks, carrying bricks, working the loom, each against a quota, for a monthly measure of barley and periodic oil and wool. Housing was institutional, movement was directed, and the ration was the thread that held it all.
nodes.src: I. J. Gelb, 'The Ancient Mesopotamian Ration System' (JNES 1965); daily labour reconstructed from the Lagash archives by Kazuya Maekawa.

nodes.label: The captive and the debtor
nodes.full: Slaves were a minority of the Sumerian workforce — mostly women weaving under guard, and men taken in war, the naked bound figures on the Standard of Ur. But the free poor could fall in too: a bad harvest, a loan at heavy interest, and a man pledged his child, then his wife, then himself against the debt. Urukagina claimed to have released some such bondsmen; the mechanism that produced them stayed in place.
nodes.src: I. J. Gelb, 'From Freedom to Slavery' (1972); debt-bondage in the Presargonic reform texts (Cooper 1986).

nodes.label: The range of women's lives
nodes.full: A Sumerian woman might run the queen's estate and exchange gifts with foreign courts, like Baranamtara of Lagash; hold high priestly office, like the en-priestess of the moon-god at Ur; own and sell land and go to law in her own name; or spend her life weaving on rations with her children beside her on the list. The distance between the top and the bottom of that range was as wide as it was for men.
nodes.src: Julia Asher-Greve, 'Frauen in altsumerischer Zeit' (1985); the en-priestess office in Joan Goodnick Westenholz's studies.

nodes.label: The soldier of the phalanx
nodes.full: The Stele of the Vultures shows him: a helmet of copper, a heavy cloak studded with metal discs, a long thrusting spear, shoulder to shoulder in a block behind a wall of rectangular shields, advancing over the enemy dead. He was a citizen called up by his city and his god, promised a share of the plunder and the reconquered land, and shown — on the same monument — as a heap of corpses under a net of circling vultures.
nodes.src: Irene Winter, 'After the Battle is Over' (1985); military equipment in Yigael Yadin, 'The Art of Warfare in Biblical Lands' (1963).

nodes.label: The scribe near the throne
nodes.full: The literate administrator stood close to power without holding it. He had spent years in the tablet house learning the sign-lists; he carried a seal of office; he turned the ruler's word into a binding record, audited the estates, and calculated the quotas. It was a craft that could be learned, that ran in families, and that gave a man of no rank a hand on the levers of the city.
nodes.src: Herman Vanstiphout, 'How Did They Learn Sumerian?' (1979); the administrative careers visible in the Lagash sealings and archives.
